name: Ethics Review with AI Assistance
title: Ethics Review with AI Assistance
answer: Ethics review with AI assistance covers the use of machine learning and natural language tools to support institutional review boards, research ethics committees, and integrity offices as they assess human subjects research, data protection, conflicts of interest, and publication ethics. It includes triage of protocols, checking consent forms for readability and required elements, flagging inconsistencies, and summarizing prior ethics decisions. It does not replace the judgment of reviewers or the authority of a committee, and it does not decide whether a study is ethical. The scope also extends to monitoring approved studies, handling amendments, and documenting the reasoning behind each recommendation.

sections.body: Ethics review with AI assistance covers the use of machine learning and natural language tools to support institutional review boards, research ethics committees, and integrity offices as they assess human subjects research, data protection, conflicts of interest, and publication ethics. It includes triage of protocols, checking consent forms for readability and required elements, flagging inconsistencies, and summarizing prior ethics decisions. It does not replace the judgment of reviewers or the authority of a committee, and it does not decide whether a study is ethical. The scope also extends to monitoring approved studies, handling amendments, and documenting the reasoning behind each recommendation.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These systems typically run on secure institutional infrastructure, either on premises or in a controlled cloud environment, because ethics files contain sensitive personal data and unpublished research plans. They may use general purpose large language models through an application programming interface, or locally hosted open models when data cannot leave the institution. The surrounding stack includes access controls, audit logs, encryption, versioned document stores, and integrations with existing ethics submission platforms. Some tools are embedded in review management software, while others are standalone assistants that produce drafts for human review.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A common workflow begins with a reviewer uploading a protocol, consent form, and supporting documents into a controlled workspace. The AI assistant then extracts key details such as study population, risks, benefits, data flows, and consent language, and compares them against the committee's checklist and prior decisions. It may produce a structured summary, highlight missing or contradictory statements, and suggest questions for the researcher, but a human reviewer verifies every point before it enters the formal record. The output is treated as a draft, not a finding, and the committee's deliberation remains the source of the final decision.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The main risks are bias in the model, overreliance on fluent but wrong summaries, leakage of sensitive information, and unclear accountability when an AI assisted review misses a problem. Provenance matters, so institutions need to record which model version was used, what documents were submitted, what prompts or settings were applied, and which human reviewer accepted or rejected each suggestion. Rights and interests of research participants, researchers, and reviewers must be protected through data minimization, consent for tool use where required, and clear policies on retention and access. The committee remains responsible for the decision, and the AI system is treated as an aid that must be auditable and contestable.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward tighter validation of AI review tools, standardized reporting of their performance, and clearer guidance from research integrity bodies. Expect more integration with ethics submission systems, better support for multilingual consent review, and routine logging that lets committees inspect how a recommendation was produced. There will also be pressure to test these tools against real review outcomes and to publish failure modes, not just accuracy claims. The likely direction is not autonomous ethics review but a documented human AI workflow where the committee's reasoning stays visible and accountable.
